symptoms: Irregular water-soaked pale to olive-green lesions rapidly turning dark purplish-brown on leaves and stems
Under humid or damp conditions, fuzzy white fungal-like growth appears on the underside of affected leaves
Stems show prominent brown to black necrotic lesions, becoming brittle
Fruit shows large, firm, greasy-looking golden-brown to dark lesions with rough surfaces
management: Treat immediately as a critical emergency; late blight can destroy an entire tomato crop within days in cool, wet weather.
Remove and safely bag infected plants or tissues immediately to arrest aerial spore drift; do not discard near greenhouses or open fields.
Contact your local agricultural extension officer or certified agronomist for PCPB-registered late blight fungicide programs (protective before rains, curative at very onset).
Avoid moving through wet foliage, which mechanically transfers zoospores across the farm.
prevention: Grow in well-ventilated structures/greenhouses or use raised beds with plastic mulch in open fields.
Ensure wide plant spacing (at least 60cm in-row, 90cm between rows) and continuous staking/trellising.
Never plant tomatoes adjacent to Irish potatoes or where volunteer potato/tomato culls remain.
Select tolerant varieties when available from certified Kenyan seed companies.
monitoring: Scout daily during prolonged cool, foggy, or rainy spells (12-22°C, RH > 90%).
Examine leaf undersides, growing tips, and fruit clusters in morning hours.
escalation: Active white sporulation detected on leaf undersides in the field.
Rapid spread to multiple plants within 48 hours following wet weather.
Fruit lesions developing across multiple ripening clusters.
kenya_notes: Extremely devastating in highland tomato production zones (e.g. Kiambu, Kirinyaga highland fringes, Nakuru, Machakos hills). Losses frequently reach 100% in untreated open fields during wet seasons.
